Your ESP32 chip isn't running at all. This is a hardware fault, not an upload problem - more re-uploading won't fix it.

What I verified:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| COM4 present? | Yes - CP210x bridge, status OK |
| esptool outside the IDE @115200 | Same "No serial data received" |
| Reset to normal boot, listen 4s | 0 bytes - not even the ROM boot message |
| Console probe ? i w to running sketch | No reply |
| WiFi scan for your NXP-AV AP | Absent (13 other networks visible) |

The key insight is that the CP210x bridge is powered from USB and enumerates independently of the ESP32. So "COM4 exists" tells you nothing about the chip. Every probe that actually touches the chip comes back silent - including the WiFi scan, which doesn't go through the serial path at all. A chip that was merely refusing to enter download mode would still be running setup() and raising NXP-AV. It isn't.

Most likely cause - your own wiring notes flag it at esp32_gateway.ino:37:

"Board must have an AMS1117 (SOT-223), not a SOT-23-5 LDO - those stop at ~6 V"

You feed 9 V straight into VIN. If that board has the SOT-23-5 regulator, 9 V killed it. Dead regulator means no 3V3, so the chip is silent while the USB-powered CP210x keeps enumerating perfectly. That matches what I measured exactly.

The one measurement that settles it - multimeter, USB plugged in, 9 V pack disconnected:

- 3V3 pin approx 3.3 V: regulator alive; check EN next (should sit near 3.3 V; if it's ~0 V something is holding reset)
- 3V3 pin approx 0 V: regulator is dead, board needs replacing

Before you plug USB in again, pull the 9 V off VIN. On most dev boards VIN and the USB 5 V rail meet at the regulator input, and 9 V there can back-feed your laptop's USB port. That's also the best explanation for your second error - the port vanishing mid-session is the board dropping off the bus, not a Windows glitch.

Two smaller things: the stray "." in "the selected serial port ." is just the IDE interpolating an empty port name after the failure - a symptom, not a cause. And it's still worth one free attempt holding BOOT through "Connecting..." - it costs nothing and would rule in the one scenario my probes can't fully separate (corrupt flash plus a broken TX line), though that needs two simultaneous faults to be true.

If the 3V3 rail reads 0 V, swap in a board with the SOT-223 AMS1117 and power it from USB alone until you've confirmed the node works - then reintroduce the 9 V feed.
3v3 pin has 3.6 and en pin 1.5

Those two numbers together confirm the overvoltage damage, and the EN reading is the direct cause of the silence.

EN = 1.5 V is why the chip is dead. The ESP32 needs EN above roughly 0.75 x VDD (~2.5 V) to come out of reset. At 1.5 V it's held in reset permanently - which is exactly the signature we measured: totally silent on serial, no AP, while the USB-powered CP210x enumerates fine.

Where 1.5 V comes from. A stock dev board has a 10 kOhm pull-up from EN to 3V3 and nothing else DC-coupled to it. To sit at 1.5 V off a 3.6 V rail, something is pulling EN down with about 7 kOhm:

  3.6 V x R / (10 kOhm + R) = 1.5 V  ->  R ~= 7 kOhm

That's not a design value - that's a leakage path. The usual culprit is the auto-reset transistor (the one RTS drives) partially conducting because it's been damaged. Your wiring schema never touches EN, so this is on-board damage, not a stray jumper.

3V3 = 3.6 V is the corroborating evidence. An AMS1117-3.3 outputs 3.3 V within a percent or two. 3.6 V is not regulation - it's the absolute maximum rating of the ESP32, and it's what you'd expect from a regulator that lost its feedback after 9 V went into a part rated for ~6 V. The two faults share one cause.

One sanity check first, because it's cheap: measure the 5 V / VIN pin with only USB connected. If it reads ~5.4 V, your meter reads about 8% high and the rail is really 3.3 V. If it reads 5.0 V while 3V3 reads 3.6 V, the regulator is genuinely out of spec.

The decisive test - jumper EN directly to 3V3 (USB only, 9 V pack off):

Use a bare wire, not a resistor. A 10 kOhm to 3V3 would parallel the existing pull-up to 5 kOhm, giving 3.6 x 7/(5+7) ~= 2.1 V - still under the threshold, so it would fail and tell you nothing. A direct wire forces the full rail and beats the ~7 kOhm leak.

Then tell me and I'll re-run the same probes. If NXP-AV appears and the console answers ?, the chip itself survived and only the reset circuit is damaged - you could keep using that board as a bench unit by flashing it with manual BOOT/EN button presses. If it stays silent with EN properly high, the chip is gone too.

Either way I would not put this board back in the car. Even in the best case you'd be running a permanently modified reset circuit off a regulator sitting at the silicon's absolute maximum. Swap in a board with the SOT-223 AMS1117, and before you reconnect the 9 V feed, confirm on the replacement that VIN actually reaches a regulator rated for it - that's the check that was missing the first time.

That settles it. The regulator is destroyed.

Here's the airtight part: a regulator can only ever output less than its nominal value when it runs out of headroom - never more. Yours is putting out 3.6 V from a 3.3 V part. There is no failure mode of a working AMS1117 that produces that. It's not regulating at all; it's passing input through a damaged pass element, dropping ~0.8 V along the way (4.4 -> 3.6).

It also answers the meter question I raised: your meter isn't reading high. If it were, the 5 V pin would have shown ~5.4 V. It showed 4.4 V - low. So 3.6 V is real, and possibly conservative.

And the 4.4 V itself is a second symptom, not a separate problem. A healthy board sits at ~4.7 V there (5 V minus the input Schottky). Sagging to 4.4 V means something is pulling serious current through the cable and that diode - consistent with a partially shorted regulator. Together with EN stuck at 1.5 V from a damaged reset transistor, that's three independent faults from one event: 9 V into a part rated for ~6 V.

Unplug it now. It's drawing enough to pull the USB rail down 0.6 V, which is unhealthy for your laptop's port, and the regulator is likely hot enough to feel. Don't leave it connected while you sort out the replacement.

Don't bother with the EN jumper test I suggested - that was to find out whether the chip survived, but with the on-board supply dead the board is scrap either way. (If you want it later as a bench unit, the salvage path is to feed a known-good 3.3 V into the 3V3 pin, bypassing the regulator entirely, and jumper EN high. Not worth it under deadline.)

Fix the design before you fit the replacement, or you'll burn that board too. Feeding 9 V straight into VIN puts the whole 5.7 V drop across the on-board LDO:

  9 V -> 3.3 V @ 150 mA  =  0.86 W   (peaks ~1.7 W on WiFi TX)
  5 V -> 3.3 V @ 150 mA  =  0.26 W

You already know this is marginal - it's why your notes say to point a fan at the regulator. That's the tell. Put a small buck module (MP1584 / LM2596) between the 9 V pack and the ESP32, set it to 5 V, and feed the 5V pin instead of VIN. The on-board LDO then dissipates a quarter as much, the fan becomes unnecessary, and it stops mattering which LDO package your next board happens to ship with - which is the actual root cause here, since that was never something you could guarantee at purchase.

Worth applying the same check to the other 9 V node: test_vis.ino:16 carries the identical "9 V logic pack direct to VIN" note, so it has the same failure waiting.

Your new board is fine - don't debug its firmware. NXP-AV is broadcasting, which means it powered up, ran setup() past Wire.begin(), and is sitting there as an I2C slave on 0x42. Both sides agree in software too: 0x42 / GPIO21 / GPIO22 match between esp32_gateway.ino:80 and the MCX config.

The number that matters in that diag line is "0 ok", not "FIFO ERROR". Your own code says so explicitly - link.c:659:

"not one poll has succeeded since this board booted, so read this as presence rather than protocol: nothing is answering at 0x42 at all"

FIFO ERROR is a red herring here, and link.c:614 explains why: on a multi-byte read, an address NAK races with the stale receive command in the FIFO, so a bus with nothing on it reports NAK and FIFO ERROR alternately. The 29->30 resets are just the recovery loop firing because nothing ever succeeds. This is a wiring fault between the two boards, not a timing or baud-rate problem - don't touch LINK_GW_BAUDRATE.

WARNING - first, before anything else: the ESP32's USB isn't connected to this laptop, but the AP is up - so this board is running on the 9 V pack through VIN, exactly like the one that just died. If you haven't confirmed this board has the SOT-223 AMS1117, you're on track to kill it too. Check that before you spend time on the I2C.

What to check, in order of likelihood given you just swapped boards:

1. The new board's pinout is probably different. This is the big one. A 30-pin ESP32 DevKit and a 36/38-pin one put GPIO21/GPIO22 in completely different physical positions. If the SDA/SCL wires went back into the same breadboard rows, they're now on the wrong pins. Count from the silkscreen labels on the new board, not from where the wires were.
2. GND. Easy to forget on a swap, and without a shared ground the bus can't work at all.
3. The 2 kOhm pull-ups to 3V3 at the MCX end (J3-8) - your notes call them "not optional and not on any board here." If they were previously borrowed from the MPU6050 module, confirm that module is still connected.
4. J5, not J6 - your notes warn J6's pins 5/6 are P1_2/P1_0, the SPI half.

The test that splits the problem in one step: plug the ESP32's USB in, open Serial Monitor at 115200, press i. That prints the gateway's own I2C counters.

- "reads 0 writes 0" means the ESP32 sees nothing on the bus either. Both ends silent = the wires between them. Confirms items 1-4 above.
- reads climbing means the ESP32 is being polled, and the fault is on the MCX's interpretation instead.

One thing worth fixing while you're in there: link.h:127 still documents FIFO ERROR as "the slave DID acknowledge and the transfer broke afterwards." The .c file explicitly overturns that - anyone reading the header first would go tune the far end's timing on a bus where nothing is connected. Want me to correct that comment?
this one has 30 pins

Two things - and one of them narrows this a lot.

First, a label check. Most 30-pin DevKits silkscreen those pins as D21/D22, not SDA/SCL. The SDA/SCL labels in your project are on the MCX end - that's what esp32_gateway.ino:34 means by "go by the silkscreen, which prints SCL and SDA" (it's talking about the mikroBUS socket). So if you verified against SDA/SCL text, make sure that wasn't only the NXP side. On the 30-pin board, right-hand header from the top:

  D23  <- top
  D22  <- SCL  (2nd)
  TX0        these two sit between them
  RX0
  D21  <- SDA  (5th)
  D19 . D18 . D5 . TX2 . RX2 . D4 . D2 . D15 . GND . 3V3

If anything landed on TX0/RX0 assuming 21 and 22 were neighbours, the bus would be empty and you'd be driving the ESP32's console UART. Worth a second look even if you're confident.

Second - the error word actually rules something out. FIFO ERROR rather than PIN LOW or BUSY tells us the bus is clocking and the lines are idling high. Per your own hints at link.c:632, missing pull-ups surface as BUSY ("SDA or SCL read LOW before the START") or PIN LOW ("a line did not come back HIGH in time"). You're getting neither. So your 2 kOhm pull-ups are fine - the master drives the bus, releases it, sends the address, and simply nothing answers.

That leaves the far end not hearing it. And my top suspect is now the ground wire, not the signal wires.

It's three wires, not two, and GND is the one you'd forget on a board swap. It matters more than usual here: your MCX is on laptop USB right now (MCU-Link COM3 is enumerated), while the ESP32 is on the 9 V pack. Separate supplies. The pull-ups are at the MCX end, referenced to MCX 3V3, so from the master's side the bus looks perfectly healthy and clocks normally - but with no shared reference the ESP32 can't resolve the levels and never ACKs. That reproduces your symptom exactly, pull-ups intact and all.

Check continuity between an ESP32 GND pin (bottom of either header) and MCX J3 pin 12 or 14.

Then settle it with the built-in test rather than more inspection - plug the ESP32's USB in, Serial Monitor at 115200, press i:

- "reads 0 writes 0" means the ESP32 has never seen a transaction. Fault is in the three wires: GND, or D21/D22 placement.
- reads climbing means it is being addressed, and the problem is on the reply path instead - a different investigation entirely.

That one keystroke tells you which half of the link to stop looking at. Paste what it prints and I'll take it from there.

That leaves the board swap as the only variable - which matches the evidence anyway: your config is identical on both sides, the bus clocks and idles high (so pull-ups are good), and the ESP32 simply never gets addressed.

Two tests that fully partition what's left.

1. Multimeter on the ESP32's D21 and D22 pins, black probe on the ESP32's own GND. Both should read ~3.3 V at idle, pulled up from the MCX end.

This is the one measurement I'd want, because it tests three things at once: signal continuity between the boards, and - because you're referencing the ESP32's own ground - the ground bond too. If SDA/SCL are truly landing on those pins and the grounds are common, 3.3 V is unavoidable. A reading near 0 V, or a drifting/floating one, means the wires aren't electrically arriving no matter which holes they're in. You said the pins match; this checks the wire behind the pin, which is a different claim.

2. Make the ESP32 tell you what it bound to. Tools > Core Debug Level > Info, reflash, and watch the boot. The core prints this from i2cSlaveInit (esp32-hal-i2c-slave.c:282):

  Initializing I2C Slave: sda=21 scl=22 freq=400000, addr=0x42

If that line appears with those values, the slave is genuinely listening on the right pins and the fault is purely physical. If it's absent, or you get "Slave Init ERROR", the slave never came up at all.

That second test matters more than it looks, because your sketch can't currently tell you either way. esp32_gateway.ino:592 discards the return value:

  Wire.begin(GW_I2C_ADDR, PIN_SDA, PIN_SCL, 400000);   // returns bool, ignored

And every failure path in that function reports only through log_e, which prints nothing at the default Core Debug Level of None. So a completely failed I2C slave still gives you a clean boot: banner, WiFi AP, working console - exactly what you're seeing. The node is structurally unable to report this particular fault, which is the same class of problem your own comment at esp32_gateway.ino:47 warns about for the borrowed pull-ups.

Want me to patch that? Checking the return and printing "I2C SLAVE INIT FAILED" in the banner is a few lines, and it would have answered this question at boot instead of after an hour of probing.

The ESP32's CP210x is gone, but there's a CH340 on COM5 - and 30-pin DevKits commonly use CH340 instead of CP210x. That may be your new board. Also NXP-AV is no longer broadcasting.

Your adapter is associated with a 5 GHz network (TP-Link_C32E_5G, 802.11ac) and is now returning only 3 networks versus 13 earlier - Windows throttles 2.4 GHz scanning while connected like that. The ESP32's AP is 2.4 GHz only, so that negative is a measurement artifact, not evidence. The earlier positive was real; this negative isn't.

So: good power, right chip, sketch running, WiFi working, I2C silent. The node is fine - nothing is reaching it.

One thing to discard, though. This banner line looks like proof that the slave initialized:

   I2C     : slave 0x42 on SDA=21 SCL=22

It isn't. esp32_gateway.ino:612 just prints the three constants - it runs identically whether Wire.begin() succeeded or failed, because the return value is discarded. That line will read exactly the same on a board with no I2C at all. It's the blind spot I mentioned, and it's why we still can't tell "wires not connected" from "slave never came up."

The test that closes this out - a boot-time probe added to setup(), before Wire.begin():

  /* Do the MCX's 2k pull-ups actually reach these pins? An external 2k to 3V3
     beats the ~45k internal pulldown; an unconnected wire cannot. */
  pinMode(PIN_SDA, INPUT_PULLDOWN);
  pinMode(PIN_SCL, INPUT_PULLDOWN);
  delay(2);
  bool sdaUp = digitalRead(PIN_SDA), sclUp = digitalRead(PIN_SCL);

  bool i2cOk = Wire.begin(GW_I2C_ADDR, PIN_SDA, PIN_SCL, 400000);   // now checked

  Serial.printf(" I2C init: %s\n", i2cOk ? "ok" : "*** Wire.begin FAILED ***");
  Serial.printf(" SDA     : %s\n", sdaUp ? "HIGH - wire + pull-up present" : "*** LOW - nothing external ***");
  Serial.printf(" SCL     : %s\n", sclUp ? "HIGH - wire + pull-up present" : "*** LOW - nothing external ***");

This splits the last remaining fork in one boot, and it does it from the ESP32's side of the wires - which is exactly the multimeter reading I asked for, without the multimeter:

- Both LOW: the wires aren't electrically arriving at those pins. Pin labels can be right while the connection isn't - a bad jumper, a dead breadboard rail, or a missing ground return.
- Both HIGH but Wire.begin FAILED: wiring is good, the slave never came up. A software fault, and I'd go at core 3.3.11's slave init next.
- Both HIGH and init ok: the ESP32 is genuinely listening and the MCX isn't reaching it. That flips the investigation to the MCX end - J5-vs-J6, and whether LPI2C is really on P3_27/P3_28.

Want me to apply this to esp32_gateway.ino and flash it to COM5? The Wire.begin() return check is worth keeping permanently either way - that's a real gap, not just a probe. Say go and I'll patch, upload, and read the result back to you.

Decisive result - and it's the third branch:

   I2C init: ok
   SDA line: HIGH - wire and pull-up present
   SCL line: HIGH - wire and pull-up present

The ESP32 is fully cleared. Wire.begin() genuinely succeeded, and both bus lines beat the internal ~45 kOhm pulldown, which only an external pull-up can do. So the wires physically reach GPIO21/22, the grounds are common, and the slave is listening at 0x42. Stop looking at this node - your wiring at the ESP32 end and its firmware are both correct.

Now, here's what that combination actually tells us. Both ends independently report a healthy idle-high bus: the ESP32 sees pull-ups, and the MCX gets NAK/FIFO (which, per your own link.c:632, requires lines that idle high - a genuinely floating bus would report PIN LOW or BUSY). Two ends both seeing pull-ups, yet neither seeing the other, is the signature of two separate buses.

Note kPORT_PullUp - the MCX enables internal pull-ups on its I2C pins, so its bus idles high whether or not anything is attached. That's why its status word looked healthy.

Both sides are now verified correct in software:

| | SCL | SDA | Address |
|---|---|---|---|
| MCX (app.h:72) | PORT3 pin 27 | PORT3 pin 28 | LPI2C0 master |
| ESP32 (boot log) | GPIO 22 | GPIO 21 | slave 0x42 |

So this is now a pure physical-wiring fault, and I can explain why it was so misleading. Each end has its own pull-ups, so each end sees a healthy bus in isolation:

  MCX  P3_27/P3_28 --[internal kPORT_PullUp]-- idles HIGH, clocks fine, "nobody ACKed"
                              break
  ESP32 GPIO21/22 --[external 2k pull-ups ]-- idles HIGH, "wire and pull-up present"

Every reading we took is true, and all of them are consistent with two disconnected buses.

What to check - from CONNECTING_THE_BOARDS.md:417, the two mikroBUS headers have this at positions 5 and 6:

| Position | J5 (I2C half) | J6 (SPI half) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | SCL - P3_27 (correct) | MISO - P1_2 (wrong) |
| 6 | SDA - P3_28 (correct) | MOSI - P1_0 (wrong) |

Wires in J6 positions 5/6 land on MISO/MOSI - geometrically identical, electrically nowhere near LPI2C0. That is precisely the trap esp32_gateway.ino:32 warns about, and it produces exactly what you're seeing. Your pull-ups sit on the wires near the MCX, so the ESP32 still sees them either way - which is why "pins are matching" can be true at the ESP32 end and the link still be dead.

Settle it with continuity, power off, probing the wire ends where they enter the MCX:

- ESP32 D22 to MCX header pin silkscreened SCL
- ESP32 D21 to MCX header pin silkscreened SDA

Go by the silkscreen letters, not by counting rows - that's what your own note meant. If those two don't beep, move the pair to the header that does.

Two housekeeping notes: the diagnostic is now flashed and lives in esp32_gateway.ino - I'd keep it, since the unchecked Wire.begin() was a real gap and those three boot lines just did the work an hour of probing couldn't. Your original is backed up at scratchpad/esp32_gateway.ino.bak if you want it reverted. Nothing is committed; the change is sitting in your working tree.
the wires are on correct pins. verified the voltage: 2.7V when sending a message

That reading changes things - and it's good news. 2.7 V means real switching activity is on the wire, since a DMM shows the time-average of a toggling line (3.3 V idle, pulled low during transfers). So the signals are reaching that point. Continuity isn't the problem after all, and my "two separate buses" conclusion was wrong.

But the ESP32 still reports reads 0. Signals arriving + slave initialized + still no ACK leaves one dominant suspect:

SDA and SCL are crossed.
